title: AgentGrad: Intervention-guided Prompt Optimization for Multi-Agent Systems
claim: Prior methods update prompts blindly with system-level feedback and randomly mixed gradients; ours targets the responsible component and clusters gradients by shared pattern.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid, conventional above ours, dashed dividers, emoji verdicts
description: The figure is split into two columns, Step 1 Gradient Extraction (blue) and Step 2 Gradient Aggregation (green). Each column has a conventional panel on top and the proposed method below, separated by a dashed line. Panel (a) shows four robot agents in a row feeding a Prediction marked with a red X. An LLM Gradient Extractor sends dashed question-mark arrows back to every agent. A red banner says the failing prompt is unknown. Panel (b) repeats the agent chain, and a hint icon is injected into Agent 4. In the second row the hint is moved to Agent 3, the prediction turns green with a check, and a curved arrow returns to Agent 3. A green banner says the target prompt is hit exactly. Panel (c) shows a cloud of mixed error cards (math, syntax, wrong fact, missed reasoning) concatenated randomly into an LLM Prompt Optimizer. Panel (d) shows an LLM Aggregator that clusters the cards into labeled groups, which feed the Optimizer. Sad and happy emoji banners carry the verdicts.
caption: Comparison of conventional textual gradient approaches and AgentGrad. In gradient extraction, conventional approaches (a) select prompts to update without identifying whose modification resolves the failure and extract gradients without agent-level intermediate supervision, while AgentGrad (b) identifies the target agent via sequential intervention and extracts gradients using the intervention-adjusted output of the target agent. In gradient aggregation, conventional approaches (c) randomly group gradients causing spurious signals, while AgentGrad (d) clusters gradients by shared patterns and abstracts them into a generalized gradient.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) achieve strong performance by employing specialized multiple agents, yet their performance depends on the prompt design of each agent. For MAS prompt optimization, textual gradient methods that guide prompt updates using natural-language feedback have emerged as a leading paradigm. In this paper, we identify limitations in two stages of existing textual gradient approaches: gradient extraction and gradient aggregation. In gradient extraction, previous works select a prompt to update without verifying whether modifying it resolves the failure, and derive gradients without agent-level supervision over the corresponding agent's intermediate output. In gradient aggregation, individual gradients are randomly grouped and concatenated, often mixing unrelated failure modes and producing prompts that fail to generalize. To address these limitations, we propose AgentGrad, a prompt optimization framework for multi-agent systems based on sequential intervention and semantic textual gradient abstraction. For each failure, sequential intervention injects a hint into one agent at a time to identify the target agent whose modification resolves the failure. The modified output of the target agent then serves as agent-level supervision for extracting a fine-grained gradient. Semantic textual gradient abstraction clusters semantically similar gradients to prevent mixing unrelated failure modes, and abstracts each cluster into a generalized gradient that captures the shared corrective pattern. Experimental results show that AgentGrad achieves state-of-the-art performance across five MAS benchmarks while reducing wall-clock optimization time by 2.5 times and optimization cost by 21.8% on average compared to the next-best baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/AgentGrad.
